title: Three perfect days in London: Soho, Kensington and Marylebone
dek: Winter Wonderland opens, the London Jazz Festival plays its final weekend, and the Swedish Church sells gingerbread and glögg. Here's a West End weekend with a cold, clear Saturday in the middle.

hero.caption: The Natural History Museum on Cromwell Road. On Saturday morning it opens at 10, and a free timed ticket gets you in ahead of the queue.

intro:
This is the weekend London turns properly towards Christmas. **Hyde Park Winter Wonderland** opens on Thursday 19 November and runs to 3 January. The Regent Street, Carnaby and Oxford Street lights have been on for a fortnight, and the hundred-odd Christmas trees on the front of the Churchill Arms in Kensington were switched on on 12 November. It's also the last weekend of the **EFG London Jazz Festival**, which ends on Sunday 22 November, so there's good music every night.

This plan stays in the West End and to the west of it, away from last week's riverside and East End route. Friday is Covent Garden and Soho: Renoir at the National Gallery, Thai grilling on Brewer Street, the Liberty Christmas shop and an early set at Ronnie Scott's. Saturday is Kensington: the Natural History Museum, lunch in the V&A's Victorian dining rooms, the Design Museum's free 10th anniversary weekend, and Branford Marsalis and Dianne Reeves playing Coltrane at Olympia. Sunday is Marylebone: the farmers' market, Churchill's paintings at the Wallace Collection in their final week, a pub roast, the Swedish Church's Christmas fair and Samara Joy at the Royal Festival Hall.

The forecast is cold and mostly dry. Friday morning may be damp after overnight rain, with a high of about 9°C. Saturday looks clear and still, with a high of 8°C and a frost overnight. Sunday is grey and around 6°C. It's dark by about 4 p.m., so this plan keeps most of each afternoon indoors and saves the streets for the lights.

days.title: Friday: Covent Garden and Soho
days.intro: Paintings in the morning, a long Soho afternoon and an early jazz set, with a late Italian supper to finish.

stops.name: Dishoom Covent Garden
stops.text: Dishoom's take on an old Bombay Irani café opens at 8 a.m., and breakfast is the calmest time to come, before the lunchtime queue forms. Order the bacon naan roll, which Time Out calls "the star of this early morning show", and a pot of chai. The room is all ceiling fans, old photographs and dark wood, and the breakfast menu has enough on it for a second round if you're hungry. From here the National Gallery is a seven-minute walk down St Martin's Lane to Trafalgar Square.

stops.name: Renoir and Love at the National Gallery
stops.text: The autumn show covers Renoir's paintings of Paris couples and crowds from the mid-1860s to the mid-1880s, and it set a ticket record for the gallery before it opened. The big loan is *Dance at the Moulin de la Galette* from the Musée d'Orsay, shown in the UK for the first time, beside the gallery's own *The Umbrellas*. Ian Mansfield of ianvisits says these are "paintings that reward a little nosiness." Standard tickets are £25; book a morning slot. On Fridays after 5:30 p.m. there are pay-what-you-wish tickets, also booked ahead.

stops.name: Kiln
stops.text: A narrow room built around a steel counter and an open grill, cooking Thai food over the flames. Order the clay pot glass noodles with pork belly and brown crab, which is the signature, plus lamb skewers and whatever curry is on. It opens all day on Fridays from noon. The counter is walk-in only and fills fast, so arrive at opening; bookings are for groups. There are no desserts, so save that for later.

stops.name: Liberty
stops.text: Walk five minutes north through Carnaby, under its Christmas lights, to the mock-Tudor department store on Great Marlborough Street, trading since 1875. This year's Christmas campaign, *The Liberty Christmas Chronicles*, runs through the windows and the store. The Christmas shop on the fourth floor is the reason to climb the creaking wooden stairs: baubles, crackers and decorations under the galleried atrium. On the way down, look at the Liberty print fabrics and the scarf hall.

stops.name: The French House
stops.text: Soho's most famous small pub was the Free French's London local during the war and later Francis Bacon's. Beer comes in halves only, apart from one day a year, so do as the regulars do and order a glass of wine or a Ricard. It's tiny and standing room only on a Friday evening, which is part of the point: the walls are covered in photographs of the writers and painters who drank here. Ronnie Scott's is three minutes away.

stops.name: Alune Wade at Ronnie Scott's
stops.text: The Senegalese bassist and singer brings *New African Orleans*, a new project linking West African music, Lagos and New Orleans brass bands, to London's best-known jazz club for the festival's last weekend. He's played with Marcus Miller, Joe Zawinul and Fatoumata Diawara. Doors open at 5:30 p.m. and he's on at 6:40. Tickets are £40 to £55 including fees, and seats near the stage go first. The early show leaves the rest of the evening free for supper.

stops.name: Bocca di Lupo
stops.text: Jacob Kenedy's Italian restaurant behind Piccadilly Circus is listed in the 2026 Michelin Guide, and it serves until midnight, which makes it the right place after a gig. The menu travels the length of Italy and tells you the region each dish comes from, in small or large portions. Michelin suggests sharing the fritti Romani while you decide. Sit at the marble counter if you can, and cross the road afterwards for a scoop at Gelupo, the team's gelato shop. Book ahead for a Friday.

days.title: Saturday: Kensington
days.intro: The clearest, coldest day. Walk through Kensington Gardens to the museums, spend the afternoon at the Design Museum, and end at Olympia for Coltrane.

stops.name: Ffiona's
stops.text: A small, candlelit neighbourhood restaurant that serves brunch on Saturdays and Sundays from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. The menu is English and generous: a full English, a Queen Scramble, eggs Benedict or a stack of buttermilk pancakes. Book a table at nine. Afterwards, walk to South Kensington through Kensington Gardens, past Kensington Palace and the Albert Memorial. It takes about half an hour and, if the forecast holds, it's the best of the weekend's daylight.

stops.name: Natural History Museum
stops.text: Alfred Waterhouse's terracotta cathedral to nature is free and open daily from 10:00 to 17:50. Book a free timed ticket to skip the weekend queue. Start in Hintze Hall under the blue whale skeleton, then go up to the second floor for **Nature and Us**, a gallery that reopened in September after 83 years shut. It's lined with old wooden filing cabinets and holds about 50 objects on how people have used and protected the natural world. Allow two hours, then cross Exhibition Road.

stops.name: V&A Café
stops.text: The V&A calls this the world's oldest museum restaurant, and the three Victorian refreshment rooms were designed by James Gamble, William Morris and Edward Poynter: tiles, stained glass and painted ceilings. The food is a straightforward cafeteria of hot dishes, salads, sandwiches, scones and tea, served from 10:00 to 17:00, so the point is the setting. The museum is free; afterwards, take the District or Circle line two stops to High Street Kensington, or a bus along Kensington Road.

stops.name: The Design Museum's 10th Anniversary Weekender
stops.text: Ten years ago the Design Museum moved into the old Commonwealth Institute, with its swooping copper-coloured roof, and this weekend it celebrates with free tours, talks and drop-in sessions. At 4:30 p.m. Yinka Ilori talks with Tim Marlow; booking is recommended. The paid show to see is **Es Devlin: Other Worlds**, the stage designer's first European retrospective, with her studio, her 30-year desk of stage work and a rotating library of 2,000 books. Timed tickets start at £17.09. The museum is open until 6 p.m.

stops.name: The Churchill Arms
stops.text: By now it's dark, which is when this Fuller's pub looks best. Its front is covered with around 90 Christmas trees and thousands of lights, a display the manager has put up for more than 30 years. Inside it's crowded and full of Churchill memorabilia. Have a pint of London Pride by the bar. There's also a Thai dining room at the back that's been serving for decades, if you'd rather stay put. Clarke's is a short walk up the same street.

stops.name: Clarke's
stops.text: Sally Clarke has run this restaurant for more than 40 years, and the 2026 Michelin Guide praises its warm hospitality and its seasonal, British-Mediterranean cooking. Expect simple, well-sourced plates that change with the market. Saturday dinner starts at 6 p.m. The restaurant takes its own bookings, so phone or book through the website and ask for the early table. Her shop across the road sells things to take home. Leave by 7:30 for Olympia, about 15 minutes by taxi.

stops.name: Branford Marsalis and Dianne Reeves Celebrate John Coltrane
stops.addr: British Airways ARC, Emberton Walk at Olympia, W14 8FJ
stops.text: This is the jazz festival's big Coltrane centenary night. Dianne Reeves sings with the Branford Marsalis Quartet in a new take on *John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman*, the 1963 album of ballads. The concert is at the British Airways ARC, the new venue in the Olympia redevelopment. Doors open at 7 p.m., and it starts at 8. Tickets are £80.50 to £88.50 including fees. Kensington (Olympia) station is next door, and taxis wait on Hammersmith Road afterwards.

days.title: Sunday: Marylebone
days.intro: A village morning in the West End: cheese, a farmers' market, Churchill's paintings and a roast, then the festival's last night.

stops.name: La Fromagerie
stops.text: Patricia Michelson's cheese shop has a walk-in cheese room and a café at the back. On Sundays the shop and café open at 9:30 a.m. Come for coffee and something from the café counter, then walk through the cheese room to choose something for later. The staff will cut, wrap and advise. The farmers' market starts at the top of the same street at ten, so you can step straight outside.

stops.name: Marylebone Farmers' Market
stops.addr: St Vincent Street and Aybrook Street, W1U 4DF
stops.text: Every Sunday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., in rain or shine, farmers and producers set up behind Marylebone High Street, with more stalls at the top of Moxon Street. In late November look for apples, root vegetables, game and cheeses, plus breads, honey and hot food. Not every stall comes every week. Some take cards, but bring a little cash and your own bag. Then it's a ten-minute walk south to Manchester Square.

stops.name: Winston Churchill: The Painter at the Wallace Collection
stops.text: This is the first big museum retrospective of Churchill's paintings since his death: more than 50 works, over half from private collections. It covers Mediterranean views, Moroccan cities, still lifes and the gardens at Chartwell. It closes next Sunday, 29 November, so it'll be busy, and tickets are £18. The rest of the house is free and open daily from 10 to 5. Don't leave without seeing Fragonard's *The Swing* and Frans Hals's *Laughing Cavalier*.

stops.name: The Coach Makers Arms
stops.text: This handsome Cubitt House pub on the crooked line of Marylebone Lane does one of the area's best Sunday lunches. Marylebone Village lists roast chicken, pork, beef and lamb with all the trimmings and Madeira gravy, served family style for tables of four or more. The kitchen runs from noon to 9 p.m. on Sundays, so there's no rush. Book a table, since Sunday lunch fills up. It's a five-minute walk from the Wallace Collection.

stops.name: The Swedish Church Christmas Fair
stops.addr: The Swedish Church, 6 Harcourt Street, W1H 4AG
stops.text: London's Swedes start Christmas with this three-day fair inside their church, run with Scandikitchen. There are stalls of gingerbread, Swedish deli food, glassware, textiles, candles and cards, and homemade glögg to drink while you queue. Entry is £3 at the door, and on Sunday it's open from 11:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Weekends get busy, so expect a short wait to get in. It's a 15-minute walk west from Marylebone Lane, or a short taxi ride.

stops.name: Daunt Books
stops.text: Walk back to the High Street for the Edwardian bookshop with the long oak galleries and the skylit back room. It's thought to be the world's first purpose-built bookshop. Books are shelved by country, guidebooks next to novels and history, so it's a good place to find something about wherever you're going next. It's open until 6 p.m. on Sundays. Buy one of the cloth bags. Then take the Bakerloo line from Baker Street to Waterloo, which takes about ten minutes.

stops.name: Samara Joy at the Royal Festival Hall
stops.text: The festival's closing night belongs to the Bronx singer who has won Grammys for her readings of the standards, in the tradition of Sarah Vaughan and Carmen McRae. She's touring her new Verve album, *Portrait*, which includes her own lyrics. Lucy-Anne Daniels, a singer rooted in gospel and jazz, opens. Doors open at 7 p.m., and the show starts at 7:30. Tickets are £53.25 to £84.75 including fees. Eat something at the Southbank Centre beforehand.

stay.name: The Langham, London
stay.text: London's grand Victorian hotel opened in 1865 at the top of Regent Street, and a renovation has brought its rooms up to the level of the best of Mayfair. Its Artesian bar has been named among the world's best bars. For this weekend the location is ideal: Marylebone's Sunday is on the doorstep, Soho is a walk down Regent Street under the lights, and Oxford Circus is five minutes away for the Bakerloo and Central lines.

stay.name: Durrants Hotel
stay.text: The Miller family has owned this hotel in four Georgian town houses since 1921. It has 92 rooms, a panelled bar and a lounge with open fires, and serves afternoon tea. Rooms at the back are quieter. It's an old-fashioned London hotel in a good way, and the Wallace Collection is across the road, with La Fromagerie and the farmers' market a few minutes' walk away.

stay.name: The Z Hotel Soho
stay.text: This hotel is in 12 converted Georgian town houses on Moor Street, at the edge of Soho, with 85 small but smart rooms. Some rooms have no windows, so ask when you book if that matters. You get free wine and cheese from 5 to 8 p.m. Ronnie Scott's, Kiln and Bocca di Lupo are all within ten minutes on foot, and Leicester Square and Tottenham Court Road stations are close.

events.name: Hyde Park Winter Wonderland opens
events.when: From Thu.; Fri. noon–10 p.m., Sat. and Sun. 10 a.m.–10 p.m.
events.text: The big Christmas fair returns with rides, an ice rink, shows and food stalls, open daily (except Christmas Day) to 3 January. Book a timed entry slot online. Entry costs £1 to £8.25 depending on the slot, and rides cost extra. Bags must be A4 or smaller.

events.name: Swedish Church Christmas Fair
events.where: The Swedish Church, 6 Harcourt Street, Marylebone
events.text: Gingerbread, glögg, candles and Swedish deli food, run with Scandikitchen. Entry is £3.

events.name: Alune Wade: New African Orleans
events.text: The Senegalese bassist's project joins West African music to New Orleans brass, as part of the London Jazz Festival.

events.name: Design Museum 10th Anniversary Weekender
events.text: Free tours, talks and workshops for the museum's tenth year in Kensington, including Yinka Ilori with Tim Marlow on Saturday at 4:30 p.m. and the Kensington Choir on Sunday at 4 p.m.

events.name: St Martin-in-the-Fields Christmas Craft Market
events.text: A weekend craft market at the church on Trafalgar Square, one of the first of the season.

events.name: Branford Marsalis and Dianne Reeves Celebrate John Coltrane
events.text: The jazz festival's Coltrane centenary concert revisits his 1963 album with Johnny Hartman.

events.name: Samara Joy closes the London Jazz Festival
events.text: The Grammy-winning singer plays songs from her new album, *Portrait*, with Lucy-Anne Daniels opening.

know: **From Heathrow (LHR):** the Piccadilly line is closed between Hammersmith and Heathrow all weekend, including Friday night. Take the Elizabeth line, which stops at Bond Street and Tottenham Court Road and takes under an hour, or the Heathrow Express to Paddington, which takes about 15 minutes. Early on Sunday the Elizabeth line is closed between Paddington and Ealing Broadway until 07:45, with fewer trains to Terminal 4. A black cab takes about an hour.

**From the other airports:** the Gatwick Express runs to Victoria, and Thameslink trains run from Gatwick and Luton Airport Parkway to Farringdon and St Pancras. The Stansted Express runs to Liverpool Street. London City Airport is on the DLR from Bank.

**Other weekend closures:** on Saturday and Sunday the District line is closed between Turnham Green and Ealing Broadway, the Bakerloo line between Queen's Park and Harrow & Wealdstone, and the Metropolitan line between Harrow-on-the-Hill and Uxbridge. On Sunday the Weaver line doesn't run until 10:15. None of these touch this plan's central routes.
**Strikes:** none are planned this weekend. The next Tube strike is due to start at noon on Thursday 26 November, so check again if you're staying on.

**Paying for transport:** tap a contactless card or phone on the yellow reader when you go in and when you come out. Use the same card or phone all day so the daily cap applies. Buses take contactless only, never cash.
**Tipping:** many restaurants add a discretionary service charge of about 12.5%. If it's on the bill, you don't need to tip again. In pubs you order and pay at the bar, and nobody expects a tip.

**Weather and light:** expect highs of 6–9°C. Friday may start damp, Saturday should be clear with a frost overnight, and Sunday looks grey. It's dark by about 4 p.m. Around Hyde Park Corner and Marble Arch, Winter Wonderland crowds build in the evenings.
